risks.note: Offshore vessels heavily depend on the oil & gas industry; fluctuations in oil prices can reduce demand for vessels and affect profitability.
Global economic slowdowns can lead to reduced investment in offshore projects, lowering utilisation rates for offshore vessels.

Offshore operations are complex and hazardous; accidents, collisions, groundings and technical failures of critical vessel systems can cause significant financial loss, costly downtime and environmental damage; adverse weather and sea conditions can also disrupt operations and damage vessels.
Vessels operating in certain regions face piracy and armed-attack risk, and political unrest (e.g., disruption around the Strait of Hormuz) can damage vessels and disrupt operations.
Increasing digitalisation of vessel operations raises the risk of cyber-attacks, which could disrupt operations or lead to data breaches.

Offshore vessels are expensive to build and maintain, financing is challenging in downturns, liquidity issues can arise if contracts aren't secured or client payments are delayed, and high operating risk drives substantial insurance premiums.
risks.risk: High capital intensity, liquidity and insurance cost risk

risks.note: Keeping pace with rapid technological advancement requires continuous, costly investment; older vessels may become obsolete under new regulations or safety norms, requiring costly upgrades or replacement.

Specialised subsea engineering, diving services and vessel operations require highly certified personnel; wage inflation or a domestic shortage of qualified marine crew/commercial divers could raise operating costs or stall execution timelines.
risks.risk: Shortage of skilled maritime crew and divers
